title: Half-empty locker
passages:
The flat bar bit into the cam at the locker's lower hinge. Miko didn't ask permission; she'd stopped asking three nodes back. The steel shrieked, a sound that pulled heads from the parts bins and the bench grinder alike. Nour didn't flinch. She stood with her arms folded, one boot braced on the drawer unit, watching the bar leverage the latch free.

"Sixty-three seals short of a full card," Nour said. Her voice carried over the grind of the bar. "You pop that, the log writes your badge to the latch and nothing else. Five minutes of shift overlap, key on the yard hook, and half the stock walks. You want that on your ticket, Miko?"

Miko grunted, shoulders driving the bar down. The cam gave with a crack. "I want to know who took them. The log swears nobody came. So either the log lies or somebody walked through the wall."

The door swung wide. Sixty-one lead-and-wire seals hung on pins stamped for a hundred twenty-four. Each seal bore a stamped number, each number written neat on the tally card clipped to the door's inner face. The pins caught the shop light, dull gray rows with gaps like missing teeth.

Nour stepped closer, close enough to smell the grease on Miko's sleeve. "Sixty-one. That's what the inventory reads. That's what the board will read when the shift-change audit hits. You just made the shortage public, loader. Congratulations."

A folded dispatch line sat in the door slot, creased sharp from the down-line run. Kettering header, Bay 4 routing, Shift 2 consignment block. Teodoro peeled it out without looking at either of them. His eyes tracked the seal numbers on the paper, then the pins, then back to the paper. He reached for the pod's plate on the bench beside Ivo's cartridge.

Teodoro lifted the pod's plate from the bench. The metal tag was warm from the bench lamp, its etched numbers sharp under the light. He held it beside the dispatch line, eyes moving line by line.

"K-7741," he read. "K-7742. K-7743. K-7744. K-7745." His finger tracked down the paper. "K-7741. K-7742. K-7743. K-7744. K-7745."

He set the plate down. The *clack* was small in the shop's hum.

"Every number on that lid came off these pins," Teodoro said. He didn't look at Nour. "Anza stock. Anza shift. Somebody walked them out the door and crimped a man into a medical pod with our own seals."

Marlowe shifted on the couch. His good hand braced the cushions; the other arm lay immobilized against his chest, the splint Teodoro had fashioned from a loader's splint kit and a length of PVC pipe. His face was pale, a scrape along the jaw darkening to bruise.

"Anza's hospitality has improved since the last time," Marlowe said. His voice was rough, the sedative still dragging at the edges. "Last time they just left me at the siding with a ration bar and a radio that didn't work."

Nour's hand closed over the tally card before Miko could pull it back. The clipboard didn't tear; Miko let it go with a sharp exhale. Nour flipped to the back page, the consignment block. Her own initials sat at the bottom of the column, neat and small: *N. Varel, Sr. Loader, Shift 1*.

She read the numbers above her signature. Bay 4. Shift 2. Four rigs. Seal ranges she'd authorized with a pen stroke and a glance at the manifest.

"Senior signs every consignment," she said. The words came flat, like she was reading a spec sheet. "I never counted what I was signing."

The shop noise didn't stop. The bench grinder kept whining. A loader's radio crackled somewhere in the bay. But the space around the locker went quiet.

Miko's flat bar hung loose in her grip. "You signed thirty-four seals out of Bay 4 last cycle," she said. "Twenty-nine the cycle before. You didn't notice the pins were light?"

Nour's thumb traced the edge of the card. "I noticed the roster stayed full. I noticed resupply came through on time. I noticed the node ate through winter." She looked up, eyes dry. "That's what I noticed."

Teodoro picked up the dispatch line again. He folded it slow, creases lining up. "The line's forger has been pulling from our stock. That means somebody here handed them over. Somebody with access to the yard hook during overlap."

"Or somebody who knew the key hung there," Miko said. "Which is everybody who's ever worked a shift change."

Ivo's cartridge ticked on the bench. 00:63:18. The numbers dropped steady, indifferent.

Rhea stood at the plate, her condition entry still glowing PENDING COUNTERSIGN. She hadn't moved since Teodoro set the pod's tag down. Her wrench rested on the bench beside the respirator parts, forgotten.

"Sixty-one seals left," Rhea said. "Sixty-three short. That's four rigs' worth, minimum. Four rigs that got crimped with Anza numbers and sent down-line clean."

"Four ghost rigs," Teodoro said. "Kass tracked four at Kettering. One vanished at 04:51."

Nour's fingers tightened on the clipboard. The card didn't leave her grip. Her initials *N. Varel* stared up under the shop lights, ink she'd laid down herself, authorizing seals she'd never touched.

Nour turned, the clipboard held against her ribs like a shield. Her boots didn't hurry. They didn't need to.

"Arithmetic," she said to the shop at large. "Signed shortage on the tally card. Frozen warrant on the board. A medical rig with its transponder cut out sitting dead at the ore siding, and a man breathing on the couch who was logged as four-twelve kilos of ballast. That flags Anza contested. Thin roster through winter. Resupply delayed. Shifts unfilled. Pell takes the box and the paper, he closes his claim, he goes home satisfied. The node survives."

She passed the bench. Ivo's cartridge ticked: 00:63:12. Rhea didn't look up from the plate.

"The card is why running fails too," Rhea said. Her voice was low, stripped of its usual edge. "You hand him over with the shortage attached, the line reads the shortage as conspiracy. Anza becomes the node that fed the forger. Every rig we touch gets audited. Every loader gets watched. We don't just lose resupply. We lose the line."

"Then we run," Miko said. She hadn't moved from the locker. The flat bar rested across her palm, forgotten. "Marlowe walks out under one of my tickets. I know a coast runner who owes me a blind berth. We're gone before the audit lands."

Nour stopped at the door. Her hand found the clipboard's edge, fingers brushing her own initials. *N. Varel, Sr. Loader, Shift 1*.

"You're doing sums with Ivo's air," Miko said. The words landed flat. "Every minute you argue, that cartridge drops. He has fifty-two minutes left. Maybe less if the patch fails. You want to trade a man for a roster spot? Fine. But don't call it arithmetic. Call it what it is."

Nour's jaw tightened. The shop held its breath. The bench grinder whined. Somewhere a radio squelched static.

"Fifty-two minutes," Nour repeated. She didn't turn. "Pell's at the north gate at oh-six-hundred with a second signature. That's eighteen minutes. He takes the pod, the warrant lifts, the board unfreezes. Resupply moves. The node eats."

She pocketed the tally card. The clipboard followed, tucked under her arm.

"Eighteen minutes," she said. "I'll walk the ballast to his cradle myself."

The door swung shut behind her.

The service rig crested the haul road at 05:59, engine note flat and heavy, no transponder chirp, no ID paint on the cab doors. Just a matte-gray tractor with a reclamation cradle welded behind the fifth wheel, empty and waiting. Pell didn't slow for the gate arm. He drove through it, the fiberglass snapping like a dry twig, and didn't glance at the shack where the night gatekeeper slept in his chair.

Teodoro's radio crackled. "North gate. Pell. Service rig, unmarked. He's not stopping."

Teodoro didn't answer. He was already moving, the dispatch line folded in one hand, the pod plate in the other, heading for the shop door.

The service rig backed toward the ore stub with the precision of something that had done this a thousand times. Air brakes hissed. The cradle's guide rails kissed the frozen ballast of the siding. Pell climbed down before the dust settled, badge 2241 clipped to his chest — Kass's badge, or a copy good enough to fool a reader at fifty meters. He carried a second warrant-token in his gloved hand, the paper stiff with official seals.

He didn't wait for Nour. Didn't wait for anyone.

Chains rattled from the rig's side boxes. Pell moved like he was alone in the yard, looping the dead med rig's tie-down points, cinching the binders with a ratchet that sang in the cold. The winch whined, a high thin sound that climbed into a growl as the med rig's frozen tires broke loose from the siding's ice.

Inside the shop, the floor plates shuddered. Tools jumped in their shadows. The bench grinder's whine dipped, caught, climbed again. Ivo's lamp on the bench threw a longer shadow as the med rig's mass dragged past the wall, steel on steel, a sound that vibrated in the fillings of your teeth.

Rhea didn't look at the lamp. She knew the number. 00:52. Fifty-two minutes of cartridge life, and the patch on Ivo's diaphragm was holding, but patches weren't fixes. They were bets.

She set her wrench down on the bench. The metal *clacked* soft against the plate.

"Rhea," Teodoro said from the doorway. He hadn't gone far. "Don't."

She didn't look at him. Her eyes tracked the winch cable disappearing through the bay door, the med rig's blunt nose emerging into the work lights, the cradle waiting hungry behind it.

"Rhea," Miko said. She was still at the locker, flat bar hooked through her belt now, hands empty. "That's a reclamation cradle. He takes the pod sealed. Lid unopened. That's the rule."

"Rules change when you stand in front of them," Rhea said.

She walked out the bay door into the work lights.

The cold hit her face, dry and sharp. The service rig's exhaust plumed sideways, acrid. The winch cable sang its high note, tension spiking as the med rig's weight came fully onto the line. Pell stood at the cradle's control pendant, thumb on the lever, watching the med rig approach. He didn't look at her.

Rhea planted her boots on the frozen gravel, directly in the cable's path. The winch line would have to pass through her to reach the cradle's fairlead.

"Hey," she called. Her voice carried over the winch. "Reclamation takes the pod sealed. That's what you said. But the pod's empty, Pell. The ballast walked out and sat on my bench and gave me a name. You're hauling a box."

Pell's head turned. Slow. The badge caught the work lights: 2241. His face was ordinary, the kind you forget before you blink. Lines at the eyes from reading manifests in bad light.

"Marlowe," he said. "Decklan Marlowe. Bay 4 loader. Discharged 21:47. Sealed as ballast. Discrepancy closed when the lid crimps." His thumb didn't move from the lever. "The warrant says ballast. The board says ballast. The second signature is in my pocket. Move."

"Board says PENDING COUNTERSIGN," Rhea said. "Mechanic's authority. Twenty minutes to shift change. You want the box? You wait for the countersign."

"Mechanic's authority doesn't override reclamation," Pell said. "Not on a frozen warrant. Not on a discrepancy. I have the token. I have the signature. I have the cradle. You have a wrench and a brother's cartridge at fifty-two minutes."

He lifted the pendant. The winch whined higher, cable tensioning.

Rhea didn't move. Her hands hung loose at her sides, empty. Behind her, the shop door framed Teodoro and Miko, motionless in the warm light.

"Fifty-two minutes," Pell said. "That's how long your brother has. That's how long this node has before the warrant lifts and the board unfreezes and resupply moves. You want to spend it standing in front of my winch?"

Rhea smiled. It wasn't nice. "I want to spend it watching you explain to the line why a living witness just got hauled off as ballast. Because that's what happens if you pull that lever. Marlowe's on the board. Alive. Crew. PENDING COUNTERSIGN. You take the pod, you take the entry. And the entry says he's a person."

Pell's thumb twitched on the lever. The winch held its note, cable screaming now, the med rig's nose inches from the cradle's guide rails.

"Then I'll take the entry too," Pell said. "Reclamation closes discrepancies. All of them."

He pulled the lever.

The cable snapped taut. The med rig lurched forward, steel grinding steel, closing the last meter to the cradle.

Rhea didn't flinch. She stepped sideways — not back, sideways — and her hand came up, flat against the med rig's cold flank as it passed. Her fingers found the hasp on the pod's lid, the lead-and-wire seal crimped tight: K-7745.

She didn't pull. She didn't cut. She just held on, one hand on the seal, her body between the winch line and the cradle, as the med rig settled into its saddle and the winch braked with a mechanical *clunk*.

Pell stared at her hand on the seal. Then at her face.

"Countersign," Rhea said. "You want the box? You need the signature. And the only seal authority within five hundred klicks just left the shop with the tally card in her pocket."

Miko left the bay without looking back at the winch. Somebody had to find the hand that walked the seals, and it wasn't going to be the two people currently arguing over a stranger's air.

The yard office sat behind the fuel point, a cinderblock box with one window gone opaque from breath and years. She shouldered the door. The shift book lived here — a ledger chained to a steel desk, its pages ruled to take two-ply forms. Two-ply: a white sheet on top, carbon beneath it, a backing sheet under that. You wrote on the white top sheet, the pen bit through, and the carbon kept a copy of everything backwards, a mirror of the hand that made it. The white sheet was the one anybody read. The carbon was the one that stayed after somebody decided the record shouldn't exist.

Last night's overlap page was gone. Not filed. Torn. A fringe of paper clung to the binding wire, and Miko ran her thumb along the tooth where the sheet had ripped free.

"Cute," she said, to nobody.

The carbon was still in the book. Whoever took the white sheet hadn't thought about the copy sweating underneath it, or hadn't cared, or had run out of the same five minutes they were trying to hide — the gap between one shift clocking out and the next clocking in, when the seal key hung on the yard hook and the latch logged no badge at all.

She lifted the carbon to the window and read it in the gray light, working each letter right to left, the way you read your own face in a dark pane. Two names pressed through the sheet, hard enough to emboss.

The first one she knew. *Doan.* The scrawl was unmistakable — Doan signed everything like the pen owed them money. Doan worked the overlap, hung the key back on the hook, and was due through the shop door inside the hour with that same key still looped on a wrist cord, none the wiser that Miko had their name folded in her jacket.

The second name she did not know.

She read it three times. It wasn't on the roster. It wasn't on the roster last cycle, or the one before. She'd worked enough overlaps at Anza to know every hand that ever touched that floor, and this was not one of them. A stranger had stood in Anza's yard office during the one window the seals could walk, and signed for the privilege.

The yard radio on the desk coughed. Teodoro's voice came through thin and far off, running the standoff out loud for anyone on the channel: winch loaded, seal K-7745, a mechanic standing in the line. Somebody laughed, the ugly kind of laugh people do when their hands don't know what else to hold.

Miko laid the carbon flat on the desk. Through the fogged window the work lights threw the shape of the service rig, the man beside it, and Rhea between them, small and not moving.

She looked again at the empty space where a second name should have been, and wasn't on any list Anza kept. Two hands had walked those seals out. One was due through the door before Ivo's cartridge ran dry. And the other belonged to somebody Miko had never met — somebody who knew exactly which five minutes at Anza were worth stealing.

Miko didn't wait for the radio to quiet. She folded the carbon, tucked it into her jacket, and walked out of the yard office into the cold. The service rig's winch had stopped. The med rig sat settled in the cradle, chains taut, Rhea's hand still on seal K-7745. Pell stood at the pendant, thumb off the lever now, watching the shop door.

The shop door opened.

Doan came through it on the stroke of six, wrist cord looped tight, the overlap locker key dangling from a carabiner against their hip. They wore the same gray coveralls they'd worn three cycles back, the same oil stain on the left cuff, the same tired set to their shoulders. They didn't look at Pell. Didn't look at Rhea. Their eyes went straight to the locker standing open in the bay, the bare pins catching the work lights.

"Sixty-one," Doan said. Not a question. A count.

They unclipped the key, walked to the locker, and ran a finger down the empty rows. The metal clicked against their nail. *Empty. Empty. Empty.*

"Sixty-three walked," they said. "Four rigs' worth. Fourteen seals a rig, two spares per bay. You do the math."

Miko stepped up beside them, close enough to smell the coffee on their breath, the grease under their nails. She pulled the carbon from her jacket and held it out, the mirror writing facing them.

Doan took it. Didn't need the window. They read it backwards the way Miko had, thumb tracing the embossed letters, and their face didn't change. No surprise. No anger. Just the flat look of somebody reading a grocery list they'd written themselves.

"Consumables," Doan said. "Down-line against resupply credit. Two lean cycles. Kept the roster fat. Kept the node eating." They handed the carbon back. "Senior signs the consignments. Shift 2 moves the stock. Everybody knows. Nobody asks."

Nour stood in the doorway behind them. She'd come back from the yard without a word, the tally card in her pocket, the clipboard under her arm. She didn't shout. Didn't move. The quiet around her was heavier than the winch had been, heavier than Pell's engine, heavier than the bench grinder's whine.

Doan looked at Nour. Looked at the clipboard. Looked at the floor.

"One hand at the far end," Doan said. "Knew the arrangement. Knew the overlap. Knew the key hung on the hook and the latch logged nobody. We only ever dealt with one."

They said the name.

Marlowe's good hand went white on the couch cushion. His breath hitched, once, sharp. The scraped jaw stopped working — stopped moving, stopped tensing, went slack in a way that had nothing to do with the sedative and everything to do with recognition.

The name hung in the shop air, between the bare pins and the frozen winch and the cartridge ticking 00:48 on the bench.

Doan didn't look at Marlowe. They looked at Miko.

"Your turn," Doan said. "What do we do with it?"
